Comfort & Fit

The Suck It England tee uses a cotton-polyester blend that lands somewhere between a vintage-soft feel and standard midweight jersey. It's not the plush, broken-in cotton you'd get from a premium blank like Next Level or Bella+Canvas, but it's perfectly comfortable for a full day of grilling, cornhole, and firework-watching. The unisex cut runs true to size with a slight athletic taper — size up if you're between sizes and prefer a looser fit.

The American Flag Tee goes 100% cotton — the classic t-shirt feel everyone knows. It's slightly heavier (around 5.3 oz), which gives it better drape and structure. The cotton breathes a bit better than the poly-blend on hot July afternoons, though it'll shrink about 3–5% on the first hot wash. If you prize that all-cotton feel, this one has the edge. The 3XL option also makes it more accessible for bigger body types.

Pro tip: For the Suck It England shirt, wash inside-out in cold water and tumble-dry low. The DTG print will stay sharp for dozens of wears. For the cotton flag tee, expect a slight vintage fade after 5–6 washes that actually makes the flag design look cooler over time.

The "Crowd Test" — Which Shirt Gets More Reactions?

We've all been there: you show up to a 4th of July party in a standard flag tee and exactly zero people comment on it. It's fine. It blends in. You look like everyone else.

The Suck It England shirt flips that script entirely. Walk into any gathering wearing George Washington throwing double birds at England, and you will get reactions. Laughs. High-fives. The one guy who wants to debate the historical accuracy of Washington's actual relationship with Britain. It's a social catalyst in garment form. For bachelor parties, tailgates, and group outings where matching shirts are involved, it's unbeatable.

The flag tee, by contrast, is the reliable workhorse. It'll never embarrass you, never draw a sideways glance from your in-laws, and never need explaining. Sometimes that's exactly what you want. But in the "fun factor" column, there's no contest.

Print Quality & Longevity

DTG printing (used on the Suck It England shirt) embeds ink directly into the fabric fibers rather than sitting on top like screen printing. The result: no cracking, no peeling, and a softer hand feel against your skin. The tradeoff is that DTG prints can lose vibrancy slightly faster than a well-cured screen print after many wash cycles. Realistically, expect 30–40 washes before any noticeable fade.

Screen printing (used on the flag tee) is the industry workhorse for a reason. The ink layer is thicker, more opaque, and holds its saturation for years. You'll retire the shirt before the print gives out. The downside is that screen prints can crack along fold lines over time if you're rough with them, especially in the dryer.
